paragraphs.text: Throughout history, dreams have often been seen as messages. Modern neuroscience, though, has been more interested in why dreams occur and what they might do for us. Surprisingly, there has also been a recent revival in the study of dream content, which is providing fascinating new insights into what we dream about, and why. According to Patrick McNamara, an expert on sleep and dreams at Boston University, our dreams do in fact have meaning.

As you sleep, you progress through five stages: two stages of light sleep, two of deep sleep, then REM (Rapid Eye Movement) sleep, which is characterized by rapid breathing (and eye movements), plus a rising heart rate. The majority of us equate dreams with REM. But dreams and nightmares also occur in stage four when you’re in a deep slow-wave sleep. McNamara has found that the kind of dreams people have in REM sleep are different from those in stage four sleep. REM dreams are more story-like, with more emotion, more aggression, and more unknown characters, he says. And it seems that these two dream stages might have different functions.

In 2009, a team of Brazilian neuroscientists reported a memory study involving a violent video game called Doom. Twenty-two players spent two nights in the lab. On the first night, they were woken during REM sleep and asked to recall their dreams, but the next night, they played Doom for an hour before bed and recounted their dreams in the morning before playing again. The scientists found that the more the players dreamed about Doom, the more their performance improved the next day – although only up to a point. This is in line with other work, showing that while a little of a stimulus can aid learning, too much can hinder it.

Robert Stickgold at Harvard Medical School, who has led a great deal of work on sleep and memory, replicated the Brazilian results, but also found that non-REM dreams can also help people seem to play a game – in this case, one involving navigating a virtual maze. But overall, the research suggests that stage four slow-wave dreams are most beneficial for declarative memories: memories for facts and events.

Meanwhile, REM sleep seems to play a bigger role in procedural memories: memories for skills that result from practice, such as riding a bike. Infants spend a much greater proportion of their time asleep, and in REM sleep especially, than adults. A one-year-old is almost constantly learning how to control his body, points out Matthew Walker from the University of California. As infants have so many skill memories to consolidate, this might explain why they need so much REM sleep.

One of the classic, and most distressing, symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is vivid nightmares. Sufferers often relive the traumatic event right after night, just as it happened. This sort of dreaming just doesn’t happen in healthy people, Stickgold says. He believes this is a window into how the healthy brain processes new emotionally-charged memories, integrating them with other memories in dreams; in patients with PTSD, that process has broken down. Walker has similar ideas. His work has shown that REM dreaming sleep, in particular, preserves negative emotional memories. In part, this is a good thing: if you don’t remember bad experiences, you can’t learn from your errors. Emotion seems to act as a flag to tell the brain an event is important to survival, so it had better remember it. Cast your mind back to distant memories, and you'll quickly realize, almost all are of an emotional nature, Walker says. That tells you the brain has done its job well. But while it’s useful to remember an unpleasant event, if you also hold on to the emotion that went with it, you’ll be left with chronic anxiety.

According to Walker’s model, during REM sleep your brain sleeps, not to remember the event, but to gradually forget the emotion so that, over time, it feels less raw. REM sleep smoothes out the sharp emotional edges, he says. It may take many nights. But think of it like polishing a stone: it's like an emotional balm for your brain at night. Why this process fails in some cases, causing PTSD, remains unclear. But it seems that more everyday stresses can also cause nightmares, says psychologist Antonio Zadra. ‘I’m convinced that frequent and distressing nightmares can be experienced by people with no history of trauma,’ he says. ‘They may react more strongly to everyday situations – like academic stress – but have not experienced real traumas either as adults or during childhood.’ In addition to aiding memory, dreams may also help us process information. Stickgold’s team recently asked volunteers to study lists of related words all connected with a central theme word that wasn’t on the list. In memory tests, the volunteers mistakenly included the theme words in their lists. When tested again after a sleep, although the number of list words they remembered fell significantly, their memory for the theme words actually improved. It looks as though the brain lets the details go, and holds onto the gist during sleep, says Stickgold. Brainwave analysis showed that REM sleep was most important for driving this. This suggests that, as well as consolidating different memories while we dream, we also extract meaning from them.
